samf-junior-1998-r2-02.title: Slide the sides
samf-junior-1998-r2-02.body:
Moving each vertical step to the outside, all the horizontal pieces on top add up to the bottom side 12, and all vertical pieces on the right add up to the left side $8+2=10$. So the perimeter equals that of a $12\times10$ rectangle: $2(12+10)=44$.

**Answer: (A) 44**

samf-junior-1998-r2-04.title: Find MP, then MQ
samf-junior-1998-r2-04.body:
Area $=\frac12\cdot PQ\cdot MP=24$, so $4\,MP=24$ and $MP=6$. By Pythagoras $MQ=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10$. The perimeter is $6+8+10=24$.

**Answer: (A) 24**

samf-junior-1998-r2-05.title: Fraction lost
samf-junior-1998-r2-05.body:
Total oranges $mp$; remaining $\frac34mp$; lost $\frac14mp$, which is $25\%$ of the total.

**Answer: (D) 25**

samf-junior-1998-r2-06.title: Nest the sheets
samf-junior-1998-r2-06.body:
The outer double sheet carries pages 1, 2, 23, 24. The next sheet inside it carries 3, 4, 21, 22. The third carries 5, 6, 19, 20. So page 6 and page 20 share a sheet with pages 5 and 19.

**Answer: (C) 5 & 19**

samf-junior-1998-r2-06.title: Pair the pages
samf-junior-1998-r2-06.body:
Pages on opposite sides of the fold add up to 25 ($6+19$, $5+20$), and each leaf holds two consecutive pages (5 and 6, 19 and 20). So the other pages are 5 and 19.

**Answer: (C) 5 & 19**

samf-junior-1998-r2-07.title: Lowest common multiple
samf-junior-1998-r2-07.body:
The marked teeth meet again when the number of teeth that have passed is a common multiple of 15 and 20. The smallest is $\operatorname{lcm}(15,20)=60$. The small gear has made $60\div15=4$ rotations (and the big one 3).

**Answer: (D) 4**

samf-junior-1998-r2-09.title: Algebra
samf-junior-1998-r2-09.body:
With length $x$ and width $y$: area $xy$, perimeter $2(x+y)$. After doubling: area $2x\cdot2y=4xy$ (4 times), perimeter $2(2x+2y)=4(x+y)$ (doubled).

**Answer: (C)**

samf-junior-1998-r2-09.title: Example
samf-junior-1998-r2-09.body:
A $2\times1$ rectangle has area 2, perimeter 6. Doubled it is $4\times2$: area 8 (4 times), perimeter 12 (doubled).

**Answer: (C)**

samf-junior-1998-r2-10.title: Add the layers
samf-junior-1998-r2-10.body:
From the top down the layers are squares: $1^2,2^2,3^2,4^2,5^2,6^2$, i.e. $1+4+9+16+25+36=91$.

**Answer: (C) 91**

samf-junior-1998-r2-11.title: Exterior angle
samf-junior-1998-r2-11.body:
The angle $n$ is an exterior angle of the triangle with angles $30^\circ$ and $180^\circ-m$, so $n=30^\circ+180^\circ-m$, i.e. $n+m=210^\circ$. With $n=\frac32m$: $\frac52m=210^\circ$ and $m=84^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $84^\circ$**

samf-junior-1998-r2-12.title: Count combinations
samf-junior-1998-r2-12.body:
Choose the pair of colours in 3 ways. For each pair, the 5 sweets split as $1+4,2+3,3+2,4+1$: 4 ways. So $3\times4=12$ learners at most.

**Answer: (B) 12**

samf-junior-1998-r2-13.title: Compare areas
samf-junior-1998-r2-13.body:
The triangle cut off has base the width $w$ of the rectangle and height $a$, so its area is $\frac12wa$. It is $\frac15$ of the rectangle: $\frac12wa=\frac15w(a+b)$, so $5a=2a+2b$, $3a=2b$ and $a:b=2:3$.

**Answer: (E) 2 : 3**

samf-junior-1998-r2-13.title: Draw a horizontal line
samf-junior-1998-r2-13.body:
Draw the horizontal line through the end of the sloping line. It splits the triangle's area exactly in half, so the upper rectangle has area $2$ and the lower one area $3$ (scaling the total to 5). Same width, so $a:b=2:3$.

**Answer: (E) 2 : 3**

samf-junior-1998-r2-14.title: Last digit cycle
samf-junior-1998-r2-14.body:
Last digits of powers of 3 repeat $3,9,7,1$ with period 4. $1998=4\cdot499+2$, so $3^{1998}$ ends in 9, and a number ending in 9 leaves remainder 4 on division by 5.

**Answer: (E) 4**

samf-junior-1998-r2-15.title: Checkerboard
samf-junior-1998-r2-15.body:
Figure $n$ is a $(2n-1)\times(2n-1)$ checkerboard with black corners, so it has $\frac{(2n-1)^2+1}{2}$ black tiles (1, 5, 13, ...). For $n=15$: $\frac{29^2+1}{2}=\frac{842}{2}=421$.

**Answer: (D) 421**

samf-junior-1998-r2-15.title: Two squares
samf-junior-1998-r2-15.body:
The black tiles form two square grids: $n^2$ on the odd rows and $(n-1)^2$ on the even rows. For $n=15$: $15^2+14^2=225+196=421$.

**Answer: (D) 421**

samf-junior-1998-r2-16.title: Closing speed
samf-junior-1998-r2-16.body:
AB turns $180^\circ$ per minute and CD turns $1080^\circ$ per minute, in opposite directions, so the angle between them closes by $1260^\circ$ per minute. The lines first coincide when this angle has closed by $90^\circ$: $t=\frac{90}{1260}=\frac1{14}$ min $=\frac{60}{14}=4\frac27$ s.

**Answer: (C) $4\frac27$**

samf-junior-1998-r2-17.title: Two equations
samf-junior-1998-r2-17.body:
Let $CD=x$ and $CY=y$. Then $x^2-y^2=30$ and (Pythagoras in triangle DCY) $x^2+y^2=100$. Adding: $2x^2=130$, $x^2=65$, so $CD=\sqrt{65}$.

**Answer: (B) $\sqrt{65}$**

samf-junior-1998-r2-18.title: Equations
samf-junior-1998-r2-18.body:
Let the weights be $s,m,l$. Then $18s+6m=5l$ and $2m+l=10s$. Multiply the second by 3: $6m=30s-3l$. Substituting: $18s+30s-3l=5l$, so $48s=8l$ and $l=6s$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

samf-junior-1998-r2-19.title: Median
samf-junior-1998-r2-19.body:
The total distance is smallest at any point between the middle two houses (the 3rd and 4th of six houses, counted from the left). Of trees A, B, C, D, only tree D lies between the 3rd and 4th houses. Moving the meeting point towards that gap reduces the sum, so tree D is the best tree.

**Answer: (D) D**

samf-junior-1998-r2-20.title: Ratios of speeds
samf-junior-1998-r2-20.body:
When B has run 100 m, C has run 80 m, so C's speed is $\frac{80}{100}=0.8$ of B's. When A finishes, B has run 90 m, so C has run $0.8\times90=72$ m and is $100-72=28$ m behind A.

**Answer: (E) 28**
